  *Provisional readings, put to the maintainer* *(all nine answered on 2026-11-02,
  decisions 420 to 428, each as built; RV-14 made each mark the decision's number)*.
  Each is pinned as built; 1 to 7 were marked provisional where the code states them
  (`399d7f6`), and 8 is the decision's own
  consequence, noted because a host sees it. RV-10's review (below) changed 4 to 7 as
  each now says and added 9, each marked provisional where the code states it; since
  RV-14 each mark is its decision's number, 420 to 428.

  1. *The instance's own `now` at a warm `restart/2`* (decision 382). The decision moves a
     timer's `last` to the resource's `now`; a timer's `last` is never later than its
     instance's (decision 188), so the instance's `now` moves with it. Nothing a host reads
     shows the instance's `now` but a timer, and an edit's give-back of a frozen timer
     (fix F11) is unchanged. (a) As built; (b) a timer's `last` alone, decision 188
     loosened for a restart.
  2. *What a forecast rise names* (decision 381). `{:dn_rises, name, {acc, pre}}` carries
     the state's `.acc`, below `.pre`, as a drop's carries it, not the `.acc` the
     catch-up will reach. (a) As built; (b) the caught-up `.acc`, capped at `.pre`.
  3. *An untest holds too* (decisions 386 and 387). The rule is applied both ways, so an
     untest holds the running configuration's own spare wiring the candidate leaves
     unwired (`k2`), which RV-3's pins had started at its var_output's initial value, and
     a point the untest rewires back to the original's unwritten var_output. (a) As
     built; (b) a test's switch only, an untest starting the original's points as before.
  4. *An instance whose type changes* (decisions 386 and 387). A point is held where the
     configuration a switch starts copies it out frozen through a connection the one it
     stops does not make, or makes of an instance it runs as another type, so that a
     point an instance the edit retypes wires through the same connection in both, `m1.aux
     k2` with `aux` written in neither type, is held too: the new type's var_output is
     another, which starts at its own initial value, as decision 347 holds one in an
     instance it retypes. Until RV-10's review this question said that such a point started
     by the edit's rules for a new type, as before; the code held it, and RV-10's review
     found the question asking about what was not built. (a) As built; (b) not held, the
     point moving to the new type's initial value at the first cycle, as before RV-10.
  5. *Decision 388's exception and reach.* A kept instance's own connection both
     configurations make is excepted, as decision 374 excepts it, since it holds the
     point's value from its first run on; "a rung reads" covers the var_output named, an
     element by its name or through a tag subscript (any element), and a word's bit,
     which is how the decision's "members" was read, a program's var_output holding no
     block, and since RV-10's review every read of its tag, a `:value` slot's and a tag
     subscript's or a bit number's in any slot, a write's among them. Since the review the
     exception holds only where the var_output holds its point's value at accept: before
     the instance's first run since a start or a restart, a warm restart keeping a
     retained point at 1 and putting the var_output at its initial 0, accept refuses it,
     naming both values, and takes it once the instance has run; and no switch starts
     such a var_output, so a restart between accept and the switch leaves it as it is,
     the point taking the var_output's value at its first copy-out while every report
     says held, as decision 374 leaves its own. (a) As built; (b) no exception, every such
     connection refused; (c) a tag subscript reading only where its range can reach the
     element; (d) after a restart since accept, the var_output started at the point's
     value, the point holding and the rung reading the hold.
  6. *Decision 389's reason, and what it drops.* Every stored sample the start lays on no
     task is dropped and reported `{name, :undeclared}`, a dropped global's reason: a
     task's own whose task the configuration declares with no single or not at all, a
     global of that name among them since RV-10's review, where it was refused as the
     image's own mistake, the image holding a global's sample only with its global; a
     global's sample no task of the configuration takes, its global kept (since the
     review, where it was dropped unreported, so no `.dropped` copy kept it); and a task's
     own of a trigger its single no longer names, which the image tells by holding no
     different sample of the task's single (since the review, where it was laid on the new
     trigger). A sample that is no bool's value, or a name that is none, is still the
     image's mistake, refused. (a) As built; (b) a reason of its own, `:no_task`, and
     another for a global's sample no task takes; (c) a global's sample no task takes
     dropped unreported, since the configuration reads it nowhere.
  7. *What decision 384 takes as a value* (decision 384). Every integer literal reads by
     its value, a based one among them, so `temps[16#3]` and `temps[2#11]` are
     `temps[3]`; a name whose subscripts are no literals is read as written. Two keys of a

  8. *A held-on `tof`'s done bit before the first scan* (decision 385). Rested by the
     restart, it reads `.dn` 0 at once: a host's `get/2` between the restart and the

- **RV-11 — the answers to RV-4's questions** (decisions 390, 391, 394, 396, 398, 399 and
  400). A restart or start whose forces file cannot be read carrying on, saying so; a
  write that timed out reported unknown until a later one lands; a clock gone wrong a
  trip; a host's requests held to their share against periodic tasks too; a device's
  open limited by an `open:` of its own; a misread address shown as the configuration
  writes it; every file write and read limited by a `write_limit:` of its own. And every
  provisional mark RV-4 left on a reading decisions 390–401 settle made the decision's
  number. It runs after RV-5 and before RV-6, whose runner code it touches.

  **RV-11 as built** (2026-11-03, branch `rv11` over `ed817b1`, with a merge of main at
  `bcab56b`, RV-14 and RV-15 landed and decisions 409–432 recorded). Each decision that
  changes something has a test that fails when it is reverted, judged by the full suite
  (the mutation table below); the leave each used, a test that pinned the reading it
  changes, changed there and only as it says, each line citing the decision, is named
  with it. No test, walk or oracle was deleted or weakened.

  - *Decision 400, a `write_limit:` of its own* (`026e49f`; `stalled_disk_test.exs`'s
    "a write the disk finishes past the idle watchdog and a poll period, within the write
    limit, lands", "the write limit is 5000 ms unless set", "each write past its limit is
    killed at the write limit, not at the idle watchdog", "a relative path's expansion is
    made within the write limit, never in the caller" and "on the real clock a force's
    write slow past the heartbeat latches no device and trips nothing"; `runner_test.exs`'s
    "a write limit out of its range"). `Logex.Runner` takes `write_limit:`, how long in
    ms of real time each file write and read of its files may take, 1 to 2147483647, 5000
    unless set; a bad value is the host's pinned `ArgumentError`, "the runner's
    write_limit: is a whole number of milliseconds, 1 to 2147483647, got: …". The default
    is the maintainer's "a few seconds": five, some twenty times the slowest store write
    RV-4 measured on a machine whose every core was busy (231 ms in 1,912) and seven times
    the most a 10 ms sleep overshot there (668 ms, RV-4's review), so that a healthy disk
    on a loaded machine meets it and a disk silent for five seconds is told stalled.
    Decision 353 stands with it in place of the idle watchdog and a poll period: a force's
    write, the store's at a trip, a stop, a shutdown, a cold restart and `start: :cold`,
    the period's write and an event's wait on it, the store's copy and its owed copy, the
    forces file's and the store's reads at a start and a restart, the look for a link,
    and a relative path's expansion, which RV-5's review left in the caller and is now
    made in a process of its own. A force's write, made while the runner runs, keeps the
    heartbeat: the runner renews every device's deadline each poll period of real time
    while it waits, leaves the wait out of the time the idle watchdog reads and takes the
    devices' notices sent meanwhile (decision 437, RV-16). `child_spec/1`'s shutdown
    is `devices * (idle + poll) + 2 * write_limit`, never less than 5000 (decision 326
    with this limit; decision 414 is RV-13's). The leave, a write limited to idle + poll:
    the tests that gave a runner a long idle watchdog only to cover its disk give
    `write_limit:` instead, `stalled_disk_test.exs`'s runners `write_limit: 1010` where
    `idle: 1000`, `retain_period_test.exs`'s hung writer `write_limit: 410` where `idle:
    400`, its messages naming the write limit; the child spec's figures; and the option
    lists `runner_test.exs` pins name `write_limit:`. The walks are on the manual clock and
    the limit is of real time: no walk stalls a disk, the file server being the whole
    VM's and the walks async, so the rule is held by `stalled_disk_test.exs`, run alone;
    the walks' writes, on the default, are the ones the landing gate of `ed817b1` saw past
    510 ms (below). Docs: `Logex.Runner`'s moduledoc ("Its write limit"),
    `Logex.Runner.Writer`'s, README's "The store on disk" and "Running a plant on the
    clock".
  - *Decision 398, an `open:` limit of its own* (`ee16f1b`, `434ada2`; `runner_test.exs`'s
    "a drive whose connect takes 600 ms opens without the heartbeat loosened", "an
    opening past its own limit is :timeout, each device's limit its own", "a device a
    restart opens again is given its own opening limit" and "an opening limit out of its
    range, or naming no device bound"). `open:`, how long in ms of real time a device's
    opening, its adapter's `init/3` and its first read, may take: a whole number from 1
    to 2147483647 for every device, or a map of device names to one, each device it names
    given its own and every other the default, 5000 ms (decision 438, RV-16). A bad
    value is the host's pinned `ArgumentError`, and a device it names that `io:` binds no
    adapter to is "the runner's open: names the device `drvie`, which io: binds no adapter
    to — did you mean `drive`?". The heartbeat stays the idle watchdog and a poll period:
    no device has heard a deadline while one opens. A device a restart opens again is
    given its own opening limit; one up is read again within the idle watchdog and a poll
    period (decision 439, RV-16). CI's first run of `ee16f1b` was red, the range test
    asserting that `open: 1` starts, where on CI the drive's opening took more than 1 ms
    and timed out as the limit says; `434ada2` asserts the least limit taken, the start
    made or timed out, never the host's mistake. No test pinned the reading changed. The
    runner walk restates it: its late open is 700 ms, past the walk's idle watchdog and a
    poll period and within the opening limit, `open:` given in half the walks by the
    seed, for every device or by name (`:late_open`). Docs: `Logex.Runner`'s moduledoc
    ("Its devices"), README's "Running a plant on the clock".

    (`2ef025c`; `runner_test.exs`'s "with no untimed program, a request made while a

  count, decision 396); a round of a runner
  with a store and a long period (nine runs) 1706.53, the parent 1704.89, 7.82 more than
  with no store against the parent's 8.05, the test's bound 10; a period's write, the

  447,205 at both, and the whole VM's over the advance that makes it through the runner
  8,652,850 against 8,645,487 (+0.09%, the wait's status polls among it); and a fresh

  `force_test.exs`, `trip_test.exs`, `retain_store_test.exs` and `runner_edit_test.exs`,
  with RV-7's write-timeout set (`force_test.exs` and `retain_store_test.exs` whole,
  `real_test.exs`'s forces file's real point and `located_array_test.exs`'s force across a
  restart), 50 runs at `1ebb4d8`: one failed, run 48, decision 396's real-clock test, its
  runner tripped, the task's watchdog then 50 ms and a 10 ms step stalled past it under

  (`scratchpad/rv/p11/disk_runs.sh`), the parent failed 3 runs of 10, `{:error,
  {:retain, :timeout}}` in `retain_store_test.exs`'s "a store's global lines are in name

  GenServer.stop whose write fails answers :ok …", and `force_test.exs`'s "a device's
  change while forced is kept", one of the seven of `ed817b1`'s landing gate, and the tip
  none of 10. So `{:forces, :timeout}` and `{:retain, :timeout}` on a healthy disk, the
  landing gate's seven and `retain_store_test.exs`'s fresh-start write at idle 500 among

  *Provisional readings, put to the maintainer* *(all eleven answered on 2026-11-04,
  decisions 437 to 447: 2, 7, 8, 10 and 11 as built, 1, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 9 changed, to build
  in RV-16)*. The record is silent on each; the reading taken is the closest to it, IEC
  and Logix.

  1. *A force on a slow disk holds the logic* (decision 400). A technician forces an
     input while the card is slow: the runner waits for the forces file's write, up to the
     write limit, 5 s, keeping every device's heartbeat, so nothing latches, but running
     no round meanwhile, every output held where it was and a 10 ms task's missed periods
     reported as overlaps. (a) As built; (b) the rounds run on while the write is in
     flight, the force taken once it lands, the write moved off the runner's own path as
     the period's is.
  2. *`open:`'s form and its default* (decision 398). A drive whose connect takes 600 ms
     opens with nothing set; a site with one slow gateway writes `open: %{"gw" => 15_000}`,
     every other card keeping 5 s. (a) As built, one number or a map by device; (b) per
     device only, beside its adapter in `io:`; (c) a longer default, Logix's 20 s
     transition to Run.
  3. *A restart's reread of a card that is up* (decision 398). A restart opens again
     only the cards that went down, each given its own `open:`; a card that stayed up is
     read again within the idle watchdog and a poll period, 510 ms, so a slow gateway that
     answers its reread in 700 ms refuses the restart with `{:io_init, "gw", :timeout}`.
     (a) As built; (b) every card a restart reads given its `open:`.
  4. *The keys that name a file not read or a write not known* (decisions 390 and 391).
     `status/1` shows `forces_unread`, `forces_unknown` and the store's `unknown` only
     while each stands, an HMI that reads them finding no key at all on a healthy plant,
     as decision 360's `copy` was shown; decision 412 has since made `copy` always present,
     nil where nothing was copied. (a) As built; (b) each always present, nil where it does
     not stand, as decision 412 has `copy`, which RV-13 could build beside it.
  5. *A clock gone wrong in the middle of a round* (decision 394). The host's clock answers
     `:error` halfway through a 10 ms task's run: the round finishes as though no time
     passed, its outputs written, and then the trip zeroes them; a time past a signed
     64-bit integer counts as gone wrong; a restart asks both the clock and, where a store
     is named, the wall clock. (a) As built; (b) the round abandoned at once, its outputs
     never written, before the trip.
  6. *The share with no continuous task* (decision 396). A plant of a 2 ms task whose
     rounds take 3 ms gives the HMI 1 ms after every 9 ms of rounds at 10%; and, since
     RV-11's review, a plant that ran timed rounds only and is edited to add a continuous
     program begins the share's count again at the edit, so its first slot comes after
     the fourth round of the continuous task at 20%, as before decision 396, where the
     count carried across the edit brought it after the first, which no record asked
     (the review's finding 6). And a slot serves the requests in the runner's queue as
     its round ends: an HMI that polls `status/1` one call at a time, each sent once the
     last is answered, finds its next call still on its way as the round ends, the slot
     gone and the count begun again, so in a 2 ms plant whose rounds take 6.7 ms it is
     answered 149 times in 2 s where the parent answered 299 (the review's finding 12),
     as the continuous task's slot has always done. (a) As built, the count begun again at
     such an edit, and an empty slot gone; (b) one count carried across the edit; (c) a
     slot that finds its queue empty keeps the count standing, so the next request is
     served at once; (d) Logix's alone, the HMI served only in the time no round needs,
     none at all while rounds outrun their periods.
  7. *An address the configuration does not write* (decision 399). An adapter that
     reports `%{pump: 1}`, a key that is no address, trips `{:unknown_address, :pump}`, as
     it gave it; and `Logex.IO.Sim.set/3` given `[7]` past its inputs refuses it naming
     `[7]`, the list the test gave, since a sim knows no device's name until a runner
     opens it. (a) As built; (b) a key that is no address shown inspected as text,
     `":pump"`, so every address a trip names is text; (c) the sim's refusal naming
     `panel.i.7` once bound.

  Put since RV-11's review, each a reading the review found unasked:

  8. *A test's call on the manual clock while a periodic round is overdue* (decisions
     131 and 396; finding 1). A box counter on a 10 ms task, no continuous program, run
     on the manual clock by a test; a slow drive's write passes 509 ms inside a round, so
     the next round is overdue, and the test then calls `status/1` from the process that
     moves the clock: the call waits for the advance that runs the round due, which that
     process never makes, so the test hangs, as a call made while a continuous task's
     round is owed always did (decision 131). (a) As built, decision 131's rule extended
     to a due periodic round, the test calling from another process; (b) a request that
     finds a periodic round overdue runs that round there and then and is served after
     it, decision 131's passed-over option, for periodic rounds or for both.
  9. *Forces the file held while a fresh start could not read it* (decisions 127 and
     390; finding 2). A technician forced the level switch to 7 and the PC crashed; the
     next start finds the disk stalled at the forces file, starts with no force and names
     the file in `status/1`; the disk recovers; at the next trip and restart the restart
     reads the file and forces the level to 7 again, a force the HMI had not listed since
     the start. (a) As built, every start takes the file (decision 127); (b) while
     `forces_unread` stands a restart keeps the runner's own set, the file taken only by
     a force's write or a fresh start, as Logix's forces live in controller memory.
  10. *A relative forces path whose directory does not answer* (decisions 390 and 400;
      finding 5). `forces: "plant.forces"` and the disk stalls as the PC boots: the start
      cannot expand the path, so it cannot claim the file, tell it from the store or
      write it, and is refused, "plant.forces: the forces file cannot be located: ...",
      where an absolute path on the same stalled disk starts with no force. (a) As built,
      refused, the words now "cannot be located"; (b) the forces file's carry-on extended:
      started with no force, the file named, the path expanded at its first write.
  11. *Which file an owed copy's killed write names* (decisions 360 and 391; finding 8).
      A retyped start whose copy of the store failed owes it; a trip's write over the
      store, the copy first, is killed at its limit while the copy's rename hangs:
      `status/1` now names the copy unknown, the store as it was, where it named the
      store, which the write never reached; and one killed in the store's own write names
      the store, the copy shown made. (a) As built, the file the write was in as its limit
      passed; (b) both files named while a copy is owed.

  *Provisional readings, put to the maintainer* *(all four answered on 2026-11-02,
  decisions 429 to 432: 1 and 2 as built, 3 and 4 changed, built by RV-15 on 2026-11-03
  and every mark made the decision's number)*. The
  record is silent on each; IEC and Logix say nothing that settles them.

  1. *The declared instance itself* (decision 403). `var x two`, `two` a block holding
     two `int[40000]` alone, is refused, told it would hold 80,001 elements: the instance
     `x` counts one, as each element of an array of instances does, and the 80,000 ints
     its type holds besides, where the item's own words named 80,000; RV-9's question 7's
     (b), which decision 403 took, counted "a block … one element". (a) As built: an
     instance counts itself, so `var x two` and `var x two[1]` both hold 80,001, and a
     block whose own `int[65536]` is at the bound compiles but no instance of it can be
     declared; (b) a declaration counts what its instance holds and not the instance:
     `var x two` at 80,000 and `var x two[1]` still 80,001, so a block holding
     `int[65536]` alone may be declared once, though not as an array of one.
  2. *A closure that is not the loader's* (decision 404). A program that calls logex's
     internal `Logex.Compiler.loaded/2` with a function of its own that gives types,
     rather than a list, is refused, told the types must be a list of function block
     types, and the function is never called, even where the types it would give are
     genuine. (a) As built; (b) the function called and each type it gives checked as
     `types:` is, so genuine types compile and one edited by hand is refused in its words.
  3. *A bit a tag numbers of a member of an element* (an observation the probes found,
     of code this item does not touch, which RV-12's review found wider). `l1` an array
     of counters, a bit a tag numbers of a member of an element, `l1[1].pv.[n]` or
     `l1[i].pv.[n]`, is compared only with the writes of that member of the same literal
     element: `ote l1[1].pv.[n]` beside `ote l1[1].pv.3` or `move 5 l1[1].pv` is warned.
     Every other pair of them that may meet is not, in either order, in an array of one
     dimension and of two, at the parent too: `ote l1[i].pv.3` beside `ote
     l1[j].pv.[n]`; `ote l1[1].pv.[n]` beside `ote l1[i].pv.3` or `move 5 l1[i].pv`; and
     `ote l1[i].pv.[n]` beside `ote l1[1].pv.[n]`, `ote l1[j].pv.[n]`, `ote l1[1].pv.3`,
     `move 5 l1[1].pv` or `move 5 l1[j].pv`; where a word array's, `ote w[i].3` beside
     `ote w[j].[n]` or `ote w[1].[n]` beside `ote w[i].3`, are warned. (a) As is, none of
     these warned; (b) warned as a word array's bits are, a bit a tag numbers meeting
     every bit of that member of every element its subscripts may name, so each pair
     above is warned, and `ote l1[1].pv.[n]` beside `ote l1[2].pv.3`, which never meet,
     is not.
  4. *A token built byte by byte* (decision 404; RV-12's review). The loader's token is
     a closure of `Logex`'s of no arguments. A host that builds one itself, byte by byte
     in the VM's external term format, from what `Logex`'s own compiled module and its
     checksum hold, can hand `Logex.Compiler.loaded/2` a type edited by hand, which
     `loaded/2` cannot tell from the loader's and compiles unchecked: the review's `seal`,
     its `xic` turned to `xio`, gives `b` 0 where the genuine gives 1. Nothing else a host
     writes passes for the token, and a program edited by hand after it compiled runs as
     it is (decision 190 checks its destinations and units, not its blocks against their
     texts), so what the token keeps is a compile's word that its blocks are their texts.
     Decision 404 says "handed in any way", and does not say whether such a term is a
     way. (a) As built, README and the moduledocs saying so; (b) no token: the loader's
     compile moved into private functions of the module that compiles, which no closure
     reaches, so no term a host can build passes for the loader's.

  after it). Decisions 403, 404 and 405 behaved as the record says: the review's 15,414
  programs of every pair of writes over word and bool arrays of one to three dimensions,

  never meet, none that meet unwarned and none new; 12,000 random programs of three to
  six writes found each program's warnings the union of its pairs'; and decision 403's
  bound held at its edge at depths 1 to 5, in arrays of one to three dimensions and
  through the loader. It found six things, each now fixed or made true:

  1. *A cost the record did not measure.* Decision 405's index of the storage bits was
     built for every array a one-shot keeps a storage bit in, up to 16 projections a bit,
     though only a write through a tag subscript looks it up, so a routine of one-shots
     on elements and no such write compiled up to 16.2% dearer than at `f31bf70`: 200
     `ons h[a,b,c].k` 16.2%, 64 `ons f[a,b,c]` 10.1%, 200 `ons w[k].b` 6.0%, 64 `ons e[k]`
     3.8%. The index is built only for the arrays some write names through a tag
     subscript, each storage bit named only then (`Logex.Warnings`' `storage_arrays/3`),
     and each of the four compiles 1.5% to 1.7% below `f31bf70`, alone and beside `ote
     z[i]`, a write through a tag subscript of another array, which with the first fix
     alone still cost 25 reductions a rung over the parent, each storage bit named before
     its array was looked at. Pinned (`tag_subscript_test.exs`, "one-shots on elements of
     arrays no write names through a tag subscript cost what they did before decision
     405"), eight programs each within 16 reductions a rung of `f31bf70`'s recorded
     compile, reverted 357 a rung over. Storage bits beside writes through a tag
     subscript, the shape the index is for, were quadratic at the parent, 3.3x and 3.6x
     as the program doubled, and are linear, 2.03x and 2.05x, 58.7% fewer at 100 of each:
     the record had said 54%, and not the growth.
  2. *The token can be forged, and the documents said it cannot.* A closure of `Logex`'s
     built byte by byte in the VM's external term format, the fun's index and old uniq

  *Provisional readings, put to the maintainer* *(all eight answered on 2026-11-07, decisions
  448 to 456, question 1 in two: 1 to 6 as built, 7 and 8 changed, to build in RV-6; and the
  refusal's bounds, decision 457, as built)*, by what an operator sees. The record is
  silent on each; the reading taken is the closest to it, IEC and Logix. Logix keeps no
  copy of a project's values across a download, and IEC 61131-3 leaves retention's medium
  to the implementer, so neither speaks to any of them.

  1. *A file made at the copy's number while the copy is written* (decision 418). A
     changed deploy's start numbers its copy `plant.retain.dropped.4`, one past the
     highest standing; in the moment it writes, a backup script drops its own
     `plant.retain.dropped.4` there. The copy is not renamed over it: the copy fails,
     `status/1` shows `failed: :eexist` and `copy: nil`, the store is held, and the next
     write over the store makes the copy as `plant.retain.dropped.5`. (a) As built,
     failed and owed, as decision 416 has a copy that cannot be made; (b) the next free
     number at once, the copy made in the same start. (A host's file named so before the
     start counts as standing and is never at the next number.) *Since RV-13's review*
     the question has a second half: the copy looks at its name raw just before its
     rename, and the rename goes through the VM's file server, which on a stalled disk
     holds it in its queue; a backup script's `plant.retain.dropped.4` dropped there in
     that moment is replaced by the copy, `status/1` showing `copy:
     "plant.retain.dropped.4"`, `failed: nil`, the script's file gone (pinned as
     provisional, decision 449 since, `stalled_disk_test.exs`'s "… after the copy looked,
     as its rename waits, is replaced"). (a) As built, the documents saying so; (b) a hard
     link to the name, which fails `:eexist` in one call where anything stands there, then
     the `.tmp` unlinked: none ever replaced, but a FAT or exFAT card, which has no hard
     links, refuses every copy, so (b) needs a fallback there, (a)'s window or (c); (c)
     the copy written straight to its name, opened exclusively, which fails where anything
     stands: none replaced, but a copy cut short by a crash is left under its number, a
     partial `plant.retain.dropped.4` an operator could put back.
  2. *An unnumbered `plant.retain.dropped` an earlier logex left* (decision 418). An
     operator upgrading finds the one copy RV-5 made beside the store. It is kept as it
     stands and counts for nothing: the first numbered copy is `plant.retain.dropped.1`.
     (a) As built; (b) taken as copy 0, so that `ls` sorts it first, nothing renamed;
     (c) renamed `plant.retain.dropped.1` by the first start that copies, its own
     numbered past it.
  3. *Two runners started at once on files that cross* (decisions 356 and 418). A
     supervisor starts line A on `a.retain` and, at the same instant, line B on
     `a.retain.dropped.2`, a name A's copies are made under. Never both run; but each
     checks the other only after its own claims are in, so both may be refused, each
     told the other's file, and the operator starts one again. (a) As built; (b)
     exactly one starts, a lock taken for every copy's name, at the cost of a second
     table the claims go through.
  4. *A copy killed before it took its number* (decisions 391 and 418). On a disk that
     stalls before the store's directory is read, a dropping start's copy is cut at the
     write limit before it chose a number: no copy can land anywhere, so `status/1` shows
     `failed: :timeout`, no `unknown`, the copy owed. One cut after it chose its number,
     in its write or rename, shows `unknown: "plant.retain.dropped.3"`. (a) As built; (b)
     `unknown` in both, naming the store's copies with no number,
     `"plant.retain.dropped.<n>"`.
  5. *A cold start over a store it cannot read* (decision 417). A store left unreadable,
     a directory in its place or a card that answers no read within the write limit:
     `start: :cold` cannot copy it, so it is refused, `{:error, {:retain, :eisdir}}` or
     `:timeout`, as a cold start whose first write fails, where it wrote a new store over
     it before (a directory refused it then too). (a) As built; (b) written over as
     before, nothing readable being lost; (c) the host's mistake, raised in the caller as
     a warm start's "the store cannot be read" is.
  6. *A cold restart over a store edited while the runner runs* (decision 417). A
     technician edits `plant.retain` by hand while the plant is tripped and then asks
     `restart(runner, :cold)`: the restart reads no store, so it copies none, and its
     write replaces the edit, as decision 284 says a hand edit made while the runner runs
     is lost. (a) As built, the copy only a start's; (b) every cold restart reads the
     store first and copies one a fresh start would refuse, at the cost of a read a
     restart.
  7. *A trip's or a cold restart's write of a very large store* (decision 414). A plant
     retaining 131,072 timers trips: the runner takes the image out and makes its text,
     some 15 s here, before the write the limit bounds, every host call waiting, and then
     writes it; only the end's write, which a supervisor's deadline bounds, makes its text
     within the write limit and is cut at it. (a) As built, the rest RV-6's (decision
     352); (b) every write's text within the limit, so that such a plant's trip, cold
     restart and `start: :cold` write fails at 5 s unless `write_limit:` is raised, a cold
     start then refused.
  8. *A start that fails after its copy, started again* (decisions 360 and 418; RV-13's
     review). A deploy that drops from the store copies it, and then its drive's device
     cannot be opened; a supervisor restarts the runner while the gateway boots, five
     times: `plant.retain.dropped.1` to `.5` stand, each the same bytes, and the sixth
     start makes `.6`. So does a copy killed past its limit that lands late, and the owed
     copy then made again (`stalled_disk_test.exs` asserts both). A store of 1 MB on a
     card fills it at a megabyte a restart. (a) As built, a copy every start that drops;
     (b) no new copy where the highest-numbered copy already holds the same bytes,
     `status/1`'s `copy` naming that one, at the cost of reading it at each such start.
  **RV-13's review** (2026-11-04, an adversarial review of `1e6718a`, every finding with

  1. *A store whose name ends in `.dropped` never counted its own copies* (medium–high).
     `Logex.Runner.Paths.copy_of/1` found a copy's number after the path's last
     `.dropped.`, by `:binary.matches/2`, whose matches never overlap: in
     `plant.dropped.dropped.1` the second `.dropped.` overlaps the first, and the name
     read as no copy. Every copy of `plant.dropped` was numbered 1, each start after the
     first that dropped failed its copy, `:eexist`, and owed it, every write over the
     store failing behind it for the run, the stop `{:error, {:retain, :eexist}}`; a
     forces file at `plant.dropped.dropped.1` was taken, and runners on `x.dropped` and
     `x.dropped.dropped.1` both started. Fixed: `copy_of/2` reads a path as a copy of a
     store given, the store's name a prefix compared whole, then `.dropped.` and decimal
     digits and nothing more, as the walk's `copies_standing/1` reads it; the numbering
     (`Logex.Runner.Writer`), the crossing claims both ways (`Paths`), the refusal's
     naming of another's copy and decision 325's refusal each give it the store they
     mean. Tests: `retain_store_test.exs`'s "a store whose name ends in `.dropped`
     numbers its copies past its own" (three starts that drop, `.dropped.dropped.1` to
     `.3`, each period's write made); the forces refusals at `plant.dropped.dropped.1`
     and `.30`; `runner_paths_test.exs`'s store at `v.dropped`'s first copy's name and
     `z.dropped` whose copy's name another holds, each refused. Each is red at
     `1e6718a`'s code.
  2. *A copy could replace a host's file at its number* (medium). The copy looks at its
     name raw and then renames through the VM's file server: a file a host makes between
     the two, as the rename waits in a held server's queue, is replaced. Decision 418
     says none is replaced; Logix and IEC are silent; the three ways to close it each
     change what an operator sees, so it is the maintainer's: question 1 above, its
     second half. The documents now say what is built: `Logex.Retain`'s comment at
     `written/2`, `Logex.Runner.Writer.copy/3`'s, the runner's moduledoc, README, §4.13
     and decisions 416's and 418's notes, a file made before the look failing the copy,
     `:eexist`, and one made between the look and the rename replaced (decision 449).
     `stalled_disk_test.exs`'s "… while it is written is never replaced" is named for
     what it shows, "… while it is written, before the copy looks at its name, is never
     replaced", its assertions as they were; and a test beside it pins the window as
     built, "… after the copy looked, as its rename waits, is replaced (provisional)",

     keeps a mark of each coil and costs six or seven reductions a coil. Pinned:
     `tag_subscript_test.exs`, "coils on members' bits no write reaches through a tag
     subscript cost what they did before decision 431", seven programs against

     a tag numbers of the latch's own element, the likelier of the two to set the latched

     bit, `otl w[1].3`, is beside either, compared with nothing. (a) As built: warned
     beside the coil through a tag subscript, quiet beside the one on its own element;
     (b) as a word array's, quiet beside both; (c) warned beside both.
  2. *Several firsts on one line* (decision 431, reframed after RV-15's review). A
     member's write is told every first a word array's write of its shape would be told,
     and where a member rule (decisions 253, 257, 288) cites another first, that one too,
     a warning both give in the same words told once: after `ote lanes[i,i].pv.[n]`,
     `move 5 lanes[j,i].pv` and `otu lanes[j,i].pv.3`, `ote lanes[1,0].pv.3` is told of
     the `ote`, the `move` and the `otu`, three warnings, where `ote w[1,0].3` on a word
     array is told of the `ote` and the `move`, two; and after `ote lanes[1].pv.3` and
     `ote lanes[i].pv.[n]`, `ote lanes[i].pv.3` is told of both, where `ote w[i].3` is
     told of the second alone. A word array's write is told of two firsts at most, a coil
     through a tag subscript and another write; a member's of three. Every first told is
     of a write that may meet it. (a) As built, each rule's first told; (b) only a word
     array's firsts where the word is judged as a word array, a member rule's own told
     only where the word array's rules tell the write nothing.
  3. *A bit a tag numbers beside its word written whole through the very tags* (decision
     431). `ote lanes[i].pv.[n]` beside `move 5 lanes[i].pv` is warned, as `ote w[i].[n]`
     beside `move 5 w[i]` is, where decision 288 leaves `ote lanes[i].pv.3` beside `move 5
     lanes[i].pv` quiet, the very tags. (a) As built, a word array's; (b) quiet, as
     decision 288's.
  4. *The check's own steps* (decision 432). `Logex.Compiler.recompiled/4` and
     `Logex.FbType.check/2`, decision 54's instruments and public for it, take the types
     and the memo they are given as checked already, as their docs say: over a block
     edited by hand `recompiled/4` gives a body that names it and holds none of its
     rungs, and `check/2` given a memo that names the edit answers for it; a compile,
     which builds its own memo and checks the body handed back as a type, refuses each.
     So nothing a host builds passes for checked through them, but they are public
     functions that trust what they are given. (a) As is; (b) both private, the check's
     walk moved into the compiler, `Logex.FbType.user?/1` the one public check.
- **RV-16 — the answers to RV-11's questions** (decisions 437, 439, 440, 441, 442 and
  445). The rounds running on while a force's write of the forces file is made, the force
  taken at the first round after it lands; every card a restart reads given its own
  `open:`; `status/1`'s `forces_unread`, `forces_unknown` and `unknown` always there; a
  round whose clock reading is found wrong abandoned, its outputs never written; a slot of
  the share that finds nothing queued kept until a request takes it; and while
  `forces_unread` stands, a restart keeping the runner's own forces. And every provisional
  mark RV-11 left on a reading decisions 437–447 settle made the decision's number. It
  runs after RV-13 and before RV-6, whose runner code both touch.
  **RV-16 as built** (2026-11-04, branch `rv16` over `da5e46e`). Each decision that
  changes something has a test that fails when it is reverted, every new test red at the
  parent's `lib/`, each judged by the full suite (the mutation table below); the leave
  each used, a test that pinned the reading it changes, changed there and only as it says,
  each changed line citing the decision, is named with it. No test, walk or oracle was
  deleted or weakened: every test line taken out is one the leave rewrote, a `refute
  Map.has_key?/2` now an assertion of nil, a value matched by `_` now the value itself, a
  pattern clause now a guard, a comment rewritten with the decision, or a walk's model of
  the reading a decision replaced, `restart_took/2` and its reach
  `:restart_took_unread_forces` now `restart_took/3` and `:restart_kept_unread_forces`.

  - *Decision 437, the rounds run on while a force's write is out* (`980904a`;
    `stalled_disk_test.exs`'s "the rounds run on while a force's write is out (decision
    437)": "rounds run, status/1 answers and the force is in effect from the first round
    after the write lands, none before", "a force asked while another's write is out waits
    behind it, its write built on the set the first left", "a trip, a restart and an
    edit's step made while it is out leave it as it was", "a stop made while it is out
    waits for it and answers its caller, every output 0", each on the manual clock with
    the VM's file server held, each given a write limit of 20 s since its load runs
    (`b2a4109`, below), the limit no part of what it reads but in the stop's second half,
    and "on the real clock the rounds run on while a force's write is out"). A force's, an
    unforce's or an unforce_all's write of the forces file is begun in a process of its
    own, `Logex.Runner.Writer.begun/2`, linked and monitored, its text made in the runner
    as before; the runner keeps `writing`, the write, the caller and the set it writes,
    and a timer of the VM's own at the write limit, `write_limit:`, counted in
    microseconds from before the process is made and rounded up to the millisecond, so
    that the limit is never short; and it goes back to its rounds. The write's exit, a
    `:DOWN`, takes the force or leaves it untaken as its answer says (`forces_landed/2`),
    each trigger it changes making its round first, and answers the caller; the timer,
    where it comes first, kills the write, `{:error, {:forces, :timeout}}`, and
    `forces_unknown` names the set, decision 391's. The write lets go of its link to the
    runner once its file call has answered, so that its exit never reaches the runner as a
    message, and a runner killed takes the write with it. Decision 400's renewal of every
    device's deadline while the runner waited on its disk is gone with the wait
    (`Writer.written/4`, `ticking/3`, `ticked/4` and the request's `waited` time), the
    rounds refreshing every device as ever; a force's request is timed against the idle
    watchdog as its own work alone, the disk's time never among it. A forces request asked
    while a write is out waits behind it, `behind`, in order, each served once the one
    before it is answered, its write built on the set that one left, so that no two are
    out at once (provisional, question 1); `status/1` lists the forces in effect, the one
    written not among them until it lands (provisional, question 2); a stop waits for the
    write to its own limit, after its zeros and its closes, answers its caller as it ends
    and gives the file up only then, a force behind it answered as to a runner that is not
    running (provisional, question 3); a trip, a restart and an edit's step leave the
    write as it is, the force taken onto the set the runner then holds, a restart reading
    the file as it stands (provisional, question 4). The walks restate it: the core's seam
    sends the forces file as each round begins (`{:on_file, ...}`), and the model asserts
    at every round that the file holds the forces the round reads (`on_file!/2`,
    `:forces_on_file`). Docs: `Logex.Runner`'s moduledoc ("Its write limit", "Forcing",
    the idle trip), `force/3`'s doc, `Logex.Runner.Writer`'s head, README's forcing,
    §4.11.
  - *Decision 439, a restart's reread limited by its device's `open:`* (`103d09e`;
    `runner_test.exs`'s "a device up that a restart reads again is given its own opening
    limit (decision 439)": a gateway that stayed up and answers its reread in 700 ms, past
    the idle watchdog and a poll period, 510 ms there, restarts, read again and not
    opened, where it was refused `:timeout`; and one hung in its reread, given `open:
    %{"drive" => 1500}`, is cut there and not at 510). A device up that a restart reads
    again is limited by its own `open:`, as one it opens again is, the release before it,
    the heartbeat and every other device call by idle + poll as before. The leave:
    `trip_test.exs`'s "a card hung in a restart's read is killed, …", which pinned the
    hung read cut at idle + poll, now given `open: 300`, the 300 ms the idle watchdog gave
    it there, so that the cut comes where it came. The runner walk restates it: at one
    restart in four, by the walk's own time, the first device up and not hung is read
    again 700 ms late in real time, its sim held, past the walk's idle watchdog and a poll
    period and within its `open:`, which refuses nothing (`late_reread/1`,
    `:late_reread`). Docs: the moduledoc ("Its devices"), `restart/2`'s doc, README's
    `open:` and restart.
  - *Decision 440, the three keys always there* (`8c94303`). `status/1` holds
    `forces_unread` and `forces_unknown` always, and the store's `retain` report `unknown`
    from every start, each nil where nothing stands, as decision 412 has `copy`. The
    leave, every pin of a key absent: `force_test.exs` (2), `stalled_disk_test.exs` (13,
    and its `written_status/2`, which waited for `unknown` to go and now for it to be
    nil), `retain_store_test.exs`'s three exact reports and `runner_test.exs`'s "status/1
    at start", each now nil; the two that matched a key present by `_` now match its
    value, the store's path and the set `%{"eye_1" => 1, "level" => 7}`. The walks restate
    it: each key read by `Map.fetch!/2`, the store's report's `unknown` asserted nil or a
    path (`retain_keys!/1`), and `copy_told/5`'s clause for an unknown copy guarded on a
    path. Docs: `status/1`'s doc, the moduledoc ("Forcing", "Its store"), README.
  - *Decision 441, a round whose clock reading is found wrong abandoned* (`4a99887`;
    `runner_test.exs`'s "a round whose clock reading goes wrong halfway through stops
    there, its outputs never written (decision 441)" and "a round that finds a device gone
    down by its own bad clock writes no device (decision 441)"; `retain_store_test.exs`'s
    "a period's write whose wall clock gives no time trips the round due with it at once
    (decision 441)"). The runner holds `in_round`, nil but inside a round, and there the
    events of the steps it has run and not yet published; from its look for a device not
    heard to its plan of the next, every reading of the runner's clock, its start's, a
    step's, a write's, its end's and with no untimed program the period's wall clock at
    its end, that gives no time the runner can hold throws the state it found (`whole/2`,
    `period_stamped/3`), and `in_round/1` publishes the round as far as it ran, its steps'
    runs kept in the resource (provisional, question 5), and trips at once, so that the
    trip's 0 is the first the devices are given after it. A step's run is put in the state
    before its time is read, so that one whose end reads wrong keeps it. A device's own
    exit by its bad clock, waiting as the round comes to its writes (`device_clocked/4`),
    stops the round there, no device written; one that goes down while the round writes is
    found by its write as before, those after it not written (provisional, question 6).
    Out of a round decision 394's rule stands, the work in hand finished and the trip
    taken as the runner next takes a message, the untimed slot's period write among it.
    The test's stand-in for the core, `WrongAfterStep`, makes the runner's next reading
    after the round's first step wrong, once; `DeviceOddClock` reads a per-process answer,
    so that one device's clock alone goes wrong. The leave: none, no test pinned the round
    run on; the comments that said so rewritten. The runner walk restates it: half the
    runner's own clock faults, by the walk's own time, come halfway through a round, after
    its step, and the round stops there, published as far as it ran, the model holding its
    steps as run (`stepped_all/2`), no device written its outputs, each device's every
    write since the round began its last outputs, a poll's write again, or the trip's
    zeros; a restart while the clock answers so refused (`runner_clock_injected/2`,
    `clock_stopped/2`, `:clock_mid_round`). Docs: the moduledoc's trip reasons and clock
    paragraph, README's trip.
  - *Decision 442, a slot that finds nothing queued kept open* (`c0b655f`;
    `runner_test.exs`'s "an open slot serves the poller's call that comes behind the round
    at once (decision 442)"). RV-11's review's figure reproduced first
    (`scratchpad/rv/p16/share.exs`, a lone poller calling `status/1` on a 2 ms plant whose
    rounds took about 10 ms on a loaded machine, two seconds): before decision 396

    `slot_open`: a slot, the continuous task's or the periodic rounds', that finds the
    queue empty stays open (`opened/1`, `periodic_slot/3`), a request that comes while a
    round is owed takes it, served at once, and the slot closes; a slot that serves its
    queue closes it, and an edit's step that begins the count again (`recounted/2`) closes
    an open one; the count begins again at each slot whether or not a request took it
    (provisional, question 7). The leave, every pin of a slot gone: `runner_test.exs`'s
    share tests, the slots' reduce, where the first of two requests sent together takes a
    slot left open since the last that served and the second waits for the next, the forty

    runner walk models the share, its count, its open slot and its queue, and asserts that
    a call made while a periodic round is due takes an open slot at once and the next
    waits (`shared/4`, `took_slot/3`, `:open_slot_taken`). Docs: the moduledoc's share and
    manual clock, README's share, §4.11.
  - *Decision 445, a restart while `forces_unread` stands keeps the runner's forces*

  - *Decision 437's order* (`stalled_disk_test.exs`'s "the forces behind a write are
    written in the order asked, a forced trigger's round between them", on a plant with
    an event task on the panel's `e`, `@kicked`). A forced trigger's write landing runs
    the trigger's round before the next force behind it is served, and that round's end
    serves the share's slot: a force that waited there for the round was served while no
    write was out, its write begun ahead of the ones behind, and the one behind it, put
    back at the tail, was written last, the older force winning (`level` 3 where 5 was
    asked last; red so at the parent). A force, an unforce or an unforce_all now waits
    behind while a write is out or while one such waits (`in_turn/3`), and the one
    behind is served by `answered_now/2`, never put back: the last asked is the last
    written. "An unforce_all waits behind a write, and a force behind a host's mistake is
    served after it" holds the unforce_all among them and the next served once a mistake
    is raised. The runner walk restates it: at one forcing step in four, by a stream of
    its own seeded by each walk (`:rw_together`, `paired/1`), so that no other draw
    moves, two to four forces of plain inputs asked together, each before the last is
    answered, the first point asked again last, and the file the order asked
    (`together/2`, `:forces_together`), red under a queue made last-in-first-out.

  *Gates and CI.* Each commit gated by `scripts/gate.sh`, GATE-OK by its exit code, one
  full suite at a time: the merge `202a9e4` 2,844; `2308f70` 2,853 (11 doctests, 2,842

  *Provisional readings, put to the maintainer* *(all eleven answered on 2026-11-08,
  decisions 465 to 475: 3, 5, 6 and 7 as built; 1, 2, 4, 8, 9, 10 and 11 changed, to build
  in RV-18)*, by what an operator sees. The record is
  silent on each; the reading taken is the closest to it, IEC and Logix. IEC 61131-3
  leaves forcing and the runtime's faults to the implementer; Logix keeps forces in the
  controller's memory, a force taking effect at the next scan once enabled, and a major
  fault stops the logic at once, its outputs going to their fault state.

  1. *A second force while the first's write is out* (decision 437). An operator forces
     `eye_1` to 1 on a disk that takes 3 s to write the file; a second, a second later,
     forces `level` to 7. As built the second waits behind the first: `eye_1` is in effect
     from the first round after its write lands, at 3 s, and `level`'s write is begun
     then, in effect from the round after it lands, at 6 s, the second HMI's call answered
     then, up to two write limits after it was made. (a) As built, in order, each write on
     the set the one before left; (b) the second refused at once while a write is out,
     `{:error, {:forces, :busy}}`, the operator forcing again; (c) every request that
     waits joined into the next write, `level`'s written with any others behind it in one
     write begun at 3 s.
  2. *What `status/1` shows while a force's write is out* (decision 437). As built
     `forces` lists the forces in effect: for the 3 s the write takes, the HMI shows
     `eye_1` unforced, as the logic reads it, and then forced. (a) As built; (b) a key of
     its own, `forcing`, the set being written, nil otherwise, so that an HMI can show
     "forcing…" beside the point.
  3. *A stop while a force's write is out* (decision 437). As built a stop zeros and
     closes every device first, then waits for the write to its own limit, answers the
     force's caller as the write answers, and answers a force waiting behind it as a
     runner that is not running; the stop returns up to the write limit later, every
     output 0 from its start, the file holding the old set or the new. (a) As built; (b)
     the write killed at once, the force answered `{:error, {:forces, :timeout}}` and the
     stop not held, the file then unknown to the next start, which reads it as it is.
  4. *A trip, a restart or an edit's step while a force's write is out* (decision 437). An
     operator forces `level` to 7; the disk stalls; the line trips on a watchdog and the
     operator restarts it while the write is still out. As built the restart reads the
     file as it stands, the old set, `level` unforced, and runs; when the write lands the
     set it wrote, built on the forces held as it began, becomes the runner's, `level` 7
     from the next round, the caller told `:ok`, and a force the restart read from the
     file that the write did not hold is dropped, the file and the forces in effect
     agreeing. RV-16's review met it so: a write cut at its limit landed late and left
     `x 1` in the file; a restart read it and `status/1` showed `x` forced; a force of
     `level` asked before the restart then landed, and the forces became `level` alone,
     `x` dropped without a word. (a) As built, the write's set the set in effect; (b) the
     write's change, `level` 7, put onto the set the runner then holds, `x` kept, and the
     file written again with that set; (c) a restart waits for the write first, so that
     it reads what the write leaves; (d) a trip cuts the write and refuses the force, the
     operator forcing again once the line runs.
  5. *An abandoned round's own work* (decision 441). The round's first step counts a box,
     `t1.boxes` 40 to 41; the runner's clock gives no time as the second step is timed,
     and the round stops there, no output written, and trips. As built the steps the round
     ran are published, `{:ran, ...}` and their events, and their runs kept in the
     resource: the count stands at 41, as `get/2` reads it, though no output was written
     of that round. (a) As built, as a Logix major fault keeps what the rungs before it
     wrote; (b) the round's work thrown away with it, the resource as the round before
     left it, `t1.boxes` 40, nothing of it published.
  6. *Where a round's clock rule ends* (decision 441). As built a round runs from its look
     for a device not heard to its plan of the next: its start's, its steps', its writes'
     and its end's readings of the runner's clock, and with no untimed program the
     period's wall clock read at its end, which trips at once. With an untimed program the
     store's period write is made in the share's slot, out of any round, so a wall clock
     gone wrong there trips as decision 394 has it, as the runner next takes a message, a
     round or a request later. And a device that goes down by its own bad clock while the
     round writes is found by its write, those written before it holding the round's
     outputs until the trip's 0 follows, those after it not written. (a) As built; (b) the
     period's write in an untimed program's slot under the same rule, tripping at once;
     (c) the round's writes held until every device's exit has been looked for, at the
     cost of a look each write.
  7. *The share's count with a slot left open* (decision 442). A 10 ms task at 10%
     overhead brings a slot every nine rounds; one finds nothing waiting and stays open;
     an HMI's call comes three rounds later and takes it at once. As built the count began
     again at the slot, so the next slot comes six rounds after the call, a second call
     close behind the first served sooner than nine rounds. (a) As built, a slot every
     nine rounds whatever takes it; (b) the count begun again when the open slot is taken,
     nine full rounds of logic between any two requests served.

  RV-16's review left four more, each where the record is silent; IEC 61131-3 says
  nothing of either forcing or a runtime's own faults, and the reading taken is the
  closest to the record and to Logix, which keeps forces in the controller's memory with
  the project and stops the logic at a major fault, outputs to their fault state.

  8. *A stop and a fresh start while `forces_unread` stands* (decisions 390 and 445). A
     level switch is forced to 7; the runner crashes; the fresh start finds the disk
     stalled, cannot read the forces file and starts with no force, `forces_unread`
     named; the disk comes back; the operator stops the line in good order and starts it
     again. As built the new start reads the file, which still holds `level 7`, and the 7
     comes back, though no one has forced it since and `status/1` never showed it:
     decision 445 keeps the runner's own set at a restart, and a stop and a start make a
     new runner that knows nothing of the old one's `forces_unread`. (a) As built, every
     fresh start reading the file as it stands, the 7 back; (b) an orderly stop while
     `forces_unread` stands writes the runner's own set to the file first, so that the
     next start finds what the HMI last showed, nothing forced; (c) as (b), and a crash's
     next start, which cannot know, as built.
  9. *A host's mistake behind a force's write* (decision 437). An HMI forces `level` to
     7 on a disk that takes 3 s to write; meanwhile a second HMI asks to force `levle`, a
     point the plant does not have. As built the mistake waits its turn behind the write,
     in order, and is raised in its caller only once the write ends, up to the write
     limit later (999 ms of a 1,000 ms limit in the review's probe); a force behind it is
     then served. (a) As built, every forces request in the order asked; (b) a request
     that is a host's mistake raised at once, as it comes, only the well-formed ones
     waiting their turn, as Logix's software refuses a tag that does not exist when it is
     typed.
  10. *The runner's own clock found wrong during or after a round's writes* (decision
      441). A conveyor's round turns its motor on, `qa` 1 to the panel, then `qb` 1 to
      the drive; the runner's clock gives no time as the drive's write is timed. As built
      nothing is written after the bad reading, the drive is never given the 1, but the
      panel already has it, and holds it until the trip's 0 follows, a moment later; and
      a clock found wrong at the round's end comes once every device has the round's
      outputs, the round's own event, `{:round, ...}`, then not published, though the
      devices got its outputs (it is published where the period's wall clock reads wrong,
      which comes after). Question 6 covers a device's own clock; this is the runner's.
      (a) As built, as a Logix major fault leaves what an output module already took
      until its fault state is applied; (b) as built, and the round's event published
      wherever any device was written, with the outputs the devices got, so that a
      subscriber's record holds the 1 the panel was given; (c) the round's end read
      before its first write, so that only a write's own reading can come once outputs
      have gone out.
  11. *A cut force write that lands after its runner has gone* (decisions 353, 356 and
      391). An operator forces `level` to 7 on a stalled disk and stops the line; the
      stop waits the write limit, cuts the write, tells the operator `{:error, {:forces,
      :timeout}}` and gives the file up; a new runner starts on the file, reads the old
      set and shows nothing forced, `forces_unknown` nil; then the disk answers and the
      cut write's rename lands, the file now `level 7`, which the next restart reads and
      puts in effect: a force the operator was told had failed (the review's probe T4).
      An unforce's late rename after a crash and a fresh start does the reverse, a force
      in effect that the file no longer holds (T5). (a) As built, documented: the file
      stands as the disk leaves it, and the next restart takes what it holds; (b) the
      file held by the runner that cut the write until the write's call has answered,
      however long the disk takes, so that no runner starts on it meanwhile (decision 356
      refuses it), the stop still answering at the limit; (c) every fresh start naming
      the forces file's set unknown, `forces_unknown`, until its own first write of it,
      where the last runner left a write cut, so that the HMI warns.
- **RV-17 — the answers to RV-13's and RV-7's questions** (decisions 459, 462 and 464).
  A ceiling a stage, the compile, a scan, a cycle and a round, under twice a figure
  recorded with it; a hold in `Logex.IO.Sim` on its next reread, and the real-clock
  reread test made to use it; `Logex.SourceFile` reading and looking at files raw. And
  every provisional mark RV-13 and RV-7 left on a reading decisions 448–464 settle made
  the decision's number. It touches no runner code and runs beside RV-6.

  **RV-17 as built** (2026-11-07, branch `rv17` over `e31a456`). Each decision has a test
  that fails when it is reverted, judged by the full suite (the mutation table below). No
  test, walk or oracle was deleted or weakened; the one test a decision changes,
  `trip_test.exs`'s real-clock reread, changed as decision 462 says, its assertions kept

  - *Decision 464, the loaders read raw* (`b490245`; `logex_test.exs`'s
    `LogexTest.HeldFileServer`, "a compile finishes while the VM's file server is held, as
    it does with it free"). `Logex.SourceFile` looks at a file with
    `:file.read_file_info/2` and reads it with `:file.read_file/2`, each `[:raw]`, and
    looks at a name beside a file with `:file.read_link_info/2`, raw, which finds a link
    to nothing and one that loops as the old look through the link and beside it did; and
    the loaders' two other calls through the server, the configuration's listing of the
    `.ld` files beside it for a did-you-mean (`File.ls/1`) and the working directory a
    relative path is expanded against for the memo's key (`Path.expand/1`'s
    `File.cwd!/0`), are `:prim_file.list_dir/1` and `:prim_file.get_cwd/0`, so that a
    compile makes no call through the server. Each answers as its call through the
    server did, a directory's read `:eisdir`, a link to nothing `:enoent`, a loop
    `:eloop`, a FIFO `:other`, a device `:device`, so the refusals and their messages are
    as they were. The test, `async: false`, compiles a program with a block beside it,
    the same by a relative path, four programs naming a FIFO, a device (`/dev/null`
    through a link, a refusal no test pinned before), a link to nothing and a link that

  - *Decision 462, a hold on the simulated device's next reread* (`e86963d`;
    `io_test.exs`'s "holds its next reread alone, until let go, a poll's read passing the
    hold by"; `trip_test.exs`'s "on the real clock, a bad reading of a device released
    while the one before it is read again trips nothing"). `Logex.IO.Sim.hold/1` arms a
    hold: the device's next reread, a restart's read of a device that stayed up (decision
    142), waits in it until `let_go/1`, and `holding?/1` says whether one waits. A reread
    is told from a poll's read by the fence `Logex.Runner.Device` sends itself just before
    it reads again, which waits in the device's mailbox, the adapter's own process, while
    the adapter reads, so that a poll, a tripped device's or a released one's, passes the
    hold by and does not spend it. The held read then goes on as usual, a failure told to
    `:read` meanwhile acted out in it, and `reads/1` counts it only then; a hold let go
    before any reread came is taken back; `hold/1` on a sim that holds already and
    `let_go/1` on one that holds nothing raise, each message pinned, and the three take a
    sim as every other call does, its mistakes pinned with theirs. The real-clock test
    holds the drive's reread, waits until it is held (every device released by then),
    tells the panel its bad reading, waits until a poll of the panel has taken it, sees
    the restart still waiting, and lets the drive go; the restart answers `:ok`, the
    runner running untripped then and two panel polls later, `x` the panel's 1. Its idle
    watchdog is 5000 ms, so that the drive's reread, held, has 5010 before the runner
    gives it up, where it was 2000 with the reread asleep 800. Red on a released device
    that passes its readings on (t4, RV-7's), on every run of three alone.
  - *Decision 459, a ceiling a stage* (`01b4afe`; `ceiling_test.exs`). One test a stage,
    each on README's motor and plant restated: the compile of `motor.ld` by
    `Logex.compile/2`; 100 scans of the motor, its start button toggled before each
    (`put_inputs/3` and `scan/3`); 100 cycles of the plant 10 ms apart, both start buttons
    toggled; and a round of the plant on the runner on the manual clock, a panel and a
    drive simulated, 200 rounds, the runner's own reductions a round less the clock's
    synchronisation (`retain_period_test.exs`'s way). Each count in a process of its own
    whose heap no collection visits, the least of five; each held under twice its figure,
    recorded with the test: compile 8,649, scans 44,606, cycles 83,262, a round 1,662
    (1,662 to 1,672 in two runs). `CONTRIBUTING.md`'s "Hold each stage under a ceiling
    twice its recorded figure" says how a figure is recorded, the least of five on the
    pinned toolchain at the commit that adds or raises it, written beside the test with
    the item and the date, and that a ceiling is raised only for a change that makes its
    stage dearer on purpose, the figure measured anew and replaced, never the factor, the
    commit saying what made it dearer; a saving may lower it.

  - *Provisional readings, and questions for the maintainer* *(all six answered on
    2026-11-08, decisions 476 to 481: 1, 4 and 6 as built, 2, 3 and 5 changed, to build in
    RV-18)*, by what a maintainer or an operator sees. The record is silent on each; the
    reading taken is the closest to it.

    1. *How the simulated device tells a restart's read* (decision 462). A test that wants
       the drive's restart read held tells its sim `hold/1`, and the sim knows that read
       by a private marker the runner's device process puts in its own mailbox just
       before a restart's read, the fence of decision 142, the newest in the mailbox and
       one no read found before since RV-17's review. If the runner's code changes
       that marker (RV-6 works there), the hold never holds, and the one test that uses
       it fails after 5 s, "no reread came to the sim's hold in 5 s", though nothing in
       the plant is wrong. (a) As built, the sim reading the device's fence, its moduledoc
       saying so; (b) the device telling its adapter that a read is a restart's, an
       optional callback of `Logex.IO` or a field the adapter is given, a change to the
       runner's code (RV-6's) and to the adapter contract; (c) a hold on the device's
       next read whatever it is, armed by the test only once it has seen the devices
       released, which a poll may still take first, the objection RV-7's question 5
       raised.
    2. *Letting go of a hold no reread came to* (decision 462). A test that calls
       `hold(drive)` and then `let_go(drive)` before any restart has read the drive gets
       `:ok`, and the hold is taken back; `hold/1` twice and `let_go/1` with nothing held
       raise. (a) As built; (b) raise there too, as the test's mistake, since a hold no
       reread came to is a test that did not do what it meant.
    3. *A working directory that cannot be read* (decision 464). A host whose working
       directory was deleted under it compiles `"lines/motor.ld"`, a relative path: the
       loader cannot make the path absolute for its memo, and raises `File.Error`,
       "could not get current working directory", as `Path.expand/1` raised it before,
       the one exception the loader lets out; an absolute path, and one from home,
       compiles as ever, since RV-17's review. (a) As built, the raise as before, its
       message `could not get current working directory nil: no such file or directory`
       pinned; (b) a `:file` diagnostic on the path, "cannot be located: the working
       directory cannot be read", as the runner tells a relative store whose directory it
       cannot resolve.
    4. *A held reread the runner gave up* (decision 462, RV-17's review). A test holds the
       drive's reread and never lets it go; at the reread's limit (the drive's `open:`
       since decision 439, 5000 ms unless set) the runner kills the drive's process and
       the restart answers `{:error, {:io_init, "drive", :timeout}}`. The
       sim then says `holding?(drive)` is false, `hold(drive)` arms again, and
       `let_go(drive)` raises "holds no reread", the hold spent on the read that died.
       (a) As built; (b) the hold armed again by itself, so that the next restart's
       reread of the drive, opened anew, would be held without a second `hold/1`; (c) as
       built, but `let_go/1` answering `:ok` once, so that a test that lets go after a
       timeout it expected is not told it made a mistake.
    5. *The loader test on a loaded machine* (decision 464, RV-17's review).
       `configuration_test.exs`'s "loading stays linear in the program types a file
       names", 250 program types loaded six times, still ran past ExUnit's 60 s in four of
       the review's ten full suites at a load average of 17 to 32, as it did before the
       loader read raw; it holds a reduction ratio, which load does not move. A
       maintainer sees one red test on a crowded CI runner and nothing wrong in logex.
       (a) As is, the record noting it; (b) its own timeout, 300 s, as the walks have;
       (c) the loader tests in a module of their own, `async: false`, run when no other
       test shares the dirty I/O schedulers (decision 464's (c)).
    6. *What a ceiling holds* (decision 459, RV-17's review). Each stage is now held
       whole, on README's motor and plant, and a rung, over the motor's five rungs written
       sixteen times over less over eight, each under twice its own figure; the decision
       names a standard program's cost alone. A maintainer whose change makes every rung's
       evaluation more than twice as dear sees `ceiling_test.exs` red on the rung, where
       the whole stage stays under its ceiling. (a) As built, both; (b) the rung alone,
       the whole stage left to the same-run bounds; (c) the whole stage alone, on a
       standard program long enough that its rungs are most of it, the motor's rungs
       written sixteen times over, one figure a stage.

  `forcing`, the set a write that is out holds; a restart waiting for a write of the
  forces file before it reads it; an orderly stop while `forces_unread` stands writing the
  runner's own set; a host's mistake in a forcing request raised at once; a round's event
  published with the outputs the devices took; and a runner's claim on its files held
